meta: Fish, plants, people and a clock tower scratched from black paint in Paul Klee's Fish Magic of 1925, in the Philadelphia Museum of Art.
about: Fish, plants, people and a clock tower float in a dark scene that Paul Klee scratched out of black paint. Under the thin black surface lies a dense layer of many colors, and Klee scrawled the figures into the dark. A square of muslin glued at the center makes the picture look like a collage. Ann Temkin points to a thin painted line running toward the clock tower, which she says seems ready to pull the muslin off. The Arensbergs gave the painting to the Philadelphia Museum of Art in 1950.

meta: A vase of pink and white flowers by Gwen John, probably from the late 1910s, one of Wales's ten iconic paintings.
about: A vase of pink and white flowers stands on a wooden table, and a few white petals have fallen onto it. A pink cloth hangs over a table behind. Gwen John painted it in oil on board with dry brushwork and thick paint, probably in the late 1910s according to her biographer Cecily Langdale. The Contemporary Art Society for Wales gave it to the National Library of Wales in 1957. In 2016 it was chosen as one of Wales's ten iconic paintings for a Europeana project.

meta: Raphael's early Portrait of a Man, painted about 1500 to 1504, once given to Holbein and to Perugino and now in the Galleria Borghese.
about: Raphael painted this portrait of a man early in his career, around 1500 to 1504. It has also been attributed to Hans Holbein and to Perugino. It was restored in 1911 and is now in the Galleria Borghese in Rome.

meta: Simonetta Vespucci in profile with a snake at her necklace in Piero di Cosimo's portrait of about 1480 in Chantilly.
about: A young woman faces left in profile, bare-breasted, with a small snake coiled round her necklace. Behind her lies a landscape, dry on the left and green on the right. Dark clouds and a dead tree are read as signs of her early death. The inscription names her Simonetta Vespucci, a Genoese noblewoman who died at 23 in 1476. Vasari saw Cleopatra in the snake. Norbert Schneider thinks it more likely stands for the cycle of time. Piero di Cosimo painted it about 1480 or 1490.

meta: William Harrison Ainsworth, friend of Dickens and author of Rookwood, painted by Daniel Maclise around 1834.
about: William Harrison Ainsworth, a popular writer of historical novels and a friend of Dickens, sits for Daniel Maclise around 1834. The portrait is very close to an illustration Maclise made for Fraser's Magazine in July 1834, the year Ainsworth's breakthrough novel Rookwood came out. An engraving of it served as the frontispiece of the novel's fourth edition two years later. The National Portrait Gallery in London acquired the painting in 1949.

meta: Monsieur Gaudry teaches his daughter geography in Louis-Léopold Boilly's 1812 painting, now in the Kimbell Art Museum.
about: Monsieur Gaudry, a friend of the painter, teaches his daughter geography in this mix of genre scene and portrait. Louis-Léopold Boilly painted it in 1812 and showed it at the Salon that year and again in 1814. The Kimbell Art Museum in Fort Worth acquired it in 1990.

meta: A girl in a canopied bed plays with a dog in Fragonard's La Gimblette, which survives in several versions.
about: A girl lies in a big canopied bed with rich linen and plays with a dog. Three versions of Fragonard's La Gimblette can be traced to the 1700s through auction catalogs, and two are now lost, so nobody can say which came first. The versions differ in how the girl wears her clothes, whether she feeds the dog a gimblette, and what kind of dog it is. In one version the dog looks like a poodle in a judge's wig, which Wikipedia says may be read as a caricature.

meta: General Rapp presents the captured Prince Repnin to Napoleon after Austerlitz in François Gérard's painting of 1810.
about: General Jean Rapp presents the captured Prince Repnin, commander of the Russian Imperial Guard, to Napoleon at the end of the Battle of Austerlitz. François Gérard painted it in 1810 on a commission of 1806, and it was first meant for the ceiling of the Council of State. Wikipedia says the picture flatters Napoleon by stressing the bravery of the guard and the Emperor's modesty rather than the enemy's defeat. It hangs in the Gallery of the Battles at Versailles.

meta: The Danish Constituent Assembly meets at Christiansborg Palace on 23 October 1848, painted by Constantin Hansen.
about: The Danish Constituent Assembly meets for the first time at Christiansborg Palace on 23 October 1848. The merchant and politician Alfred Hage ordered the painting from Constantin Hansen. Twelve years had passed, so Hansen worked from old photographs, drawings and even busts to paint the many portraits. He finished it in late 1864 or early 1865. Hage showed it at home for two weeks, and 2,898 people paid to see it, with the money going to veterans of the Second Schleswig War. His widow gave it to the Museum of National History at Frederiksborg Castle.

meta: The Virgin and Child above four saints in Perugino's Madonna in Glory with Saints, painted about 1500 for a chapel in Bologna.
about: The Virgin and Child sit inside an almond-shaped glow above four saints on a hilly landscape. From the left they are the Archangel Michael in decorated armor, Catherine of Alexandria with her wheel, Apollonia with the pincers of her martyrdom and John the Evangelist with his eagle. Pietro Perugino painted it around 1500 to 1501 for the Scarani Chapel in San Giovanni in Monte, and signed it on Catherine's wheel. It is now in the Pinacoteca Nazionale in Bologna.

meta: The Virgin holds the Christ Child in a dead tree in Petrus Christus's Madonna of the Dry Tree, painted about 1462 to 1465.
about: The Virgin stands in the fork of a dead tree and holds the Christ Child, while black, withered branches curl around her like a crown of thorns. Fifteen golden letter As hang from the branches, perhaps for the Angelus or the Ave Maria. Petrus Christus painted the small oak panel about 1462 to 1465. It was not attributed to him until 1919, when Grete Ring linked it to his style. Its size suggests private prayer, and the imagery may relate to a Bruges confraternity of Our Lady of the Dry Tree that Christus and his wife joined.

meta: Louis XV ordered Jean-François de Troy's Oyster Dinner of 1735 for Versailles, with what Wikipedia calls the first champagne bottle in painting.
about: A party eats oysters in this picture by Jean-François de Troy, which Wikipedia says includes the first champagne bottle in painting. Louis XV ordered it in 1735 for the dining room of his small apartments at Versailles, as a pair to Nicolas Lancret's The Ham Dinner. De Troy was not paid until 1738. The Duke of Aumale bought it in 1857 for 3,000 francs, and both paintings are now in the Musée Condé at Chantilly.

meta: Hans Holbein the Younger's small self-portrait drawing of about 1542, bought in London for Cosimo III de' Medici and now in the Uffizi.
about: Hans Holbein the Younger looks straight out of this small drawing, and the art historian Stephanie Buck says the direct gaze suggests he used a mirror. It dates from about 1542 to 1543, not long before he died, probably of the plague. The sheet has been enlarged and heavily reworked, and the gold background and the inscription were added later. Copies exist, including one by Lucas Horenbout that shows Holbein holding a paintbrush. Cosimo III de' Medici had it bought in London in 1681.

meta: A little girl in a blue armchair, painted by Mary Cassatt in 1878 with changes by Degas, rejected by the World's Fair.
about: A little girl sits in a big blue armchair in this painting by Mary Cassatt. Edgar Degas made some changes to it. Cassatt sent it to the American section of the 1878 World's Fair in Paris, and to her annoyance it was rejected. It was probably shown at the Impressionist exhibition of 1879, which she had joined after the Salon turned down her work. The National Gallery of Art in Washington owns it.

meta: Christ on the cross against a gold ground with grieving angels, attributed to Giotto, about 1315, in Strasbourg.
about: Christ hangs on a cross against a plain gold ground, with grieving angels crowded around him and Mary Magdalene in red embracing the cross below. At the left a group of women supports the fainting Mary. The panel is dated about 1315. Roberto Longhi gave it to Giotto in 1948, and critics are still unsure, though the 2013 Giotto exhibition at the Louvre attributed it to him without doubt. It probably formed a diptych with a Madonna now in a New York collection.

meta: Magdalena Ventura, the bearded lady, nurses her baby beside her husband in Jusepe de Ribera's 1631 painting in the Prado.
about: Magdalena Ventura stands nursing her baby, with a long untrimmed beard, while her husband, with a neatly trimmed one, stands behind her in the shadows. Two stone tablets on the right tell her story in Latin and call it a wonder of nature. They say she was 52 and that her beard began to grow when she was 37. Jusepe de Ribera painted it in 1631, reportedly for the Duke of Alcalá, who had heard rumors about her. It hangs in the Prado.

meta: Cima da Conegliano's Madonna and Child in a Landscape of 1496 to 1499, one of at least five made from a single cartoon.
about: Cima da Conegliano usually made one-of-a-kind works, but this Madonna and Child in a landscape, painted between 1496 and 1499, seems to belong to a group of at least five made from a single cartoon. It is now in the Los Angeles County Museum of Art.

meta: Saint Stephen preaches before an imagined Constantinople standing in for Jerusalem in Vittore Carpaccio's painting of 1514, now in the Louvre.
about: Saint Stephen preaches in Jerusalem, and Vittore Carpaccio fills the canvas with picturesque eastern costumes and buildings. His Jerusalem is really an imagined Constantinople, mixing Turkish and antique elements with Byzantine and Italian ones. It was one of five scenes from the saint's life painted for the Scuola dei Lanieri in Venice. The series was broken up in 1806. This panel went to the Louvre in an exchange in 1812, while others went to Milan and Berlin, one is in Stuttgart, and one has disappeared.

meta: A man in black reads a tiny book against a wooded background in Correggio's portrait of about 1522, in Milan.
about: A man in a black coat and cap reads from a tiny book in his right hand, standing against a wooded background. Roberto Longhi thought it a book of hours, while others read it as a miniature Petrarch, in which case the bee in the background could refer to two of the poems. Correggio painted it about 1522 directly on top of the sketch, a casual technique that suggests it was for a close friend. It is sometimes given to Parmigianino. It was left to the Castello Sforzesco in Milan in 1945.

meta: Saint Jerome reads in the desert beside a crucifix in Giovanni Bellini's painting of about 1480 in the Uffizi.
about: Saint Jerome reads in the desert beside a crucifix on a long shaft, which he used to help him pray. His lion is there, with birds, a lizard, a squirrel on a branch and one deer chasing another, all probably symbolic. Behind him rises a walled town with guard towers and bell towers, some based on buildings Bellini had seen in Romagna, among them San Vitale in Ravenna. Giovanni Bellini painted it around 1480, and it is in the Uffizi.

meta: Thirsty sheep stampede toward a dam while a drover tries to turn them in Tom Roberts's A break away! of 1891.
about: Thirsty sheep stampede toward a dam while a drover on horseback tries to turn the mob before they drown or crush each other. Tom Roberts painted A break away! at Corowa in 1891, in a time of drought. Arthur Streeton recalled that Roberts travelled for six weeks with the drovers to paint it. The Art Gallery of South Australia bought it in 1899. It has been called an icon of Australian art.

meta: The wind god and the thunder god on folding screens: Ogata Kōrin's replica of a work by Tawaraya Sōtatsu, painted around 1700.
about: The wind god and the thunder god appear on a pair of folding screens painted on gold-foil paper, each more than four metres wide. Ogata Kōrin painted them around 1700 as a replica of a similar work by Tawaraya Sōtatsu. Sakai Hōitsu later owned the screens and painted Flowering Plants of Summer and Autumn on the back. The two sides have since been separated to protect them. The screens are an Important Cultural Property of Japan.

meta: The three kings kneel before the Virgin and Child in Sandro Botticelli's Adoration of the Magi, made around 1475 for Gaspare del Lama.
about: The three kings kneel before the Virgin and the newborn Jesus, with Joseph behind them and a crowd around, in Sandro Botticelli's altarpiece for the chapel of Gaspare di Zanobi del Lama in Santa Maria Novella, painted around 1475. Wikipedia says the crowd includes prominent members of the Medici family and the patron himself. Gaspare was a Florentine banker and broker, the son of a barber from Empoli. His name is the Italian form of Caspar, one of the magi, which may partly explain the choice of subject.
